nature-clim-212.title: Stratospheric aerosols: copying a volcano
nature-clim-212.text: Volcanic eruptions release sulfates into the upper atmosphere, and the planet cools. Stratospheric aerosol injection would do this on purpose, putting small reflective particles high up to reflect sunlight. Sulfates are the usual proposal for that reason. It is the most-researched form of solar radiation modification, and the IPCC found high agreement that it could limit warming to below 1.5 °C. A key risk is delaying the recovery of the ozone layer.

nature-clim-214.title: Termination shock: the danger of stopping
nature-clim-214.text: Solar radiation modification masks warming rather than removing its cause. Stop it suddenly while greenhouse gas levels are high, and the hidden warming would arrive fast. This termination shock would bring rapid temperature rise, sea level rise and weaker carbon sinks. Large-scale use would likely need a commitment of decades to a century. The IPCC notes that a gradual phase-out alongside mitigation would reduce the impact.

nature-clim-184.title: BiCRS: storing the carbon in plant waste
nature-clim-184.text: Direct air capture is costly and energy-hungry. Biomass carbon removal and storage, or BiCRS, lets photosynthesis do the capturing instead. It collects biomass such as farm waste, then uses engineering to store its carbon-rich residue permanently or semi-permanently. The family includes BECCS and biochar carbon removal. Challenges include measuring the carbon stored in buried biomass and extra demand for farmland, so think tanks urge limits on which biomass may be used.

nature-clim-181.title: Biochar carbon credits
nature-clim-181.text: In 2024, biochar projects made up 86% of the volume of carbon dioxide removal purchases. Their certified removals are sold as biochar carbon credits in carbon markets. Because abatement costs are high, these credits trade about an order of magnitude above credits from emission cuts or nature-based solutions. To be certified, suppliers must be carbon net-negative, storing more carbon than they use making and distributing the biochar.

nature-clim-167.title: The energy transition: leaving fossil fuels behind
nature-clim-167.text: Energy production and use cause most human greenhouse gas emissions, and fossil fuels still meet over three-quarters of energy needs. An energy transition is a major structural change in how energy is supplied and used. Today it means the shift from fossil fuels to renewable and low-carbon energy. The current transition aims to cut energy emissions mainly by phasing down fossil fuels and running as much as possible on low-carbon electricity. It is not the first. During the Industrial Revolution, societies moved from wood and biomass to coal, then to oil and gas. The term itself arose after the 1973 oil crisis, and Jimmy Carter popularized it in 1977. Since the late 2010s, falling solar and wind costs have driven the change. Yet progress is slow. Despite decades of climate policy, transitions have not sped up beyond historical trends, and they remain off track for climate targets.

nature-clim-215.title: Sustainable energy: meeting needs without borrowing from the future
nature-clim-215.text: Fossil fuels provide 85% of world energy use, and the energy system causes 76% of greenhouse gas emissions. Sustainable energy is energy that meets present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs. It is judged by its effects on environment, economy and society. Those effects range from greenhouse gas emissions and air pollution to energy poverty and toxic waste. Around 790 million people still lack electricity, and 2.6 billion cook with polluting fuels such as wood or charcoal. Renewables such as wind, hydro, solar and geothermal can harm the environment, but they are generally far more sustainable than fossil fuels. Whether non-renewables belong is disputed. Nuclear avoids carbon and air pollution but brings waste, proliferation and accident risks. Efficiency matters as much as supply: the IEA says it could deliver 40% of the emission cuts the Paris Agreement needs. The bill is large. The IPCC estimates US$2.4 trillion a year must be invested in energy from 2016 to 2035 to limit warming to 1.5 °C.

nature-clim-174.title: Just transition: leaving no one behind
nature-clim-174.text: In the 1980s, US trade unions sought protection for workers hit by environmental rules. Tony Mazzocchi of the Oil, Chemical and Atomic Workers Union proposed a 'Superfund for Workers' to compensate and retrain them, and is believed to have coined the term just transition. The principle holds that the shift to a low-carbon economy should treat people fairly and leave no workers, places or countries behind. Unions won just transition and decent work language in the Paris Agreement's preamble in 2015. The IPCC stresses low-emission industries, fair jobs, equitable energy access and economic diversification. As of 2022, 38% of 170 countries mentioned it in their short-term climate plans. The EU's Just Transition mechanism helps regions dependent on fossil fuels move to a greener economy.

nature-clim-197.title: Phasing out fossil fuels
nature-clim-197.text: Fossil fuels cause over 70% of greenhouse gas emissions, so phasing them out is the largest part of limiting warming. The proposal is a gradual reduction of their use and production to zero, to cut air pollution, limit climate change and gain energy independence. Policies include demand-side measures that cut consumption and supply-side measures that limit production. Alternatives include electrification, green hydrogen and biofuel. Most premature deaths from air pollution are due to fossil fuels, and the health benefits of phase-out, valued in money, exceed the cost of the 2 °C goal. Governments still subsidized fossil fuels by about $500 billion a year as of 2019, and the IMF's wider definition gave $5.2 trillion in 2017. As of 2024, global fossil fuel use was still rising, as it has since 1965. Workers and politicians tied to fossil industries tend to oppose phase-out unless they have strong alternatives.

nature-clim-193.title: Electrification: running the world on clean power
nature-clim-193.text: The National Academy of Engineering called electrification the greatest engineering achievement of the 20th Century. Electrification means switching to electricity as the power source. In sustainable energy, it means moving end uses such as transport and heating onto clean electricity. The reason is simple. Clean energy such as renewables and nuclear is mostly produced as electricity, so end uses must be electrified for a sustainable system. Electric vehicles and heat pumps are two key areas. Electrification and economic growth are highly correlated, and 1900 to 1940 was a period of high productivity growth. Access is still uneven. About 840 million people, mostly in Africa, had no grid electricity in 2017, down from 1.2 billion in 2010. Electricity is a 'sticky', multi-source form of energy. It is resilient in the long term but unstable in the short term, because supply must match use instantly.

nature-clim-172.title: Energy justice: who gains and who pays
nature-clim-172.text: Cities often gain from energy systems while rural areas bear the burdens. Energy justice aims for communities to gain affordable, safe and sustainable energy and to take part in decisions about it. It seeks to share benefits and burdens fairly across social groups, regions and generations. Its three main tenets are distributive justice, recognition justice and procedural justice. Distributive justice concerns how revenues, infrastructure sites and costs are shared. Recognition justice asks who is ignored. Procedural justice requires transparent decisions and meaningful consultation. Some scholars add restorative and cosmopolitan justice to capture international inequalities and harms from fossil fuels. The energy justice cycle follows the system from extraction through production, supply and consumption to decommissioning and waste. The stakes are real, because transitions may worsen energy insecurity for low-income households.

nature-clim-169.title: The collapsing cost of wind, solar and batteries
nature-clim-169.text: From 2010 to 2019, unit costs fell 85% for solar, 55% for wind and 85% for lithium-ion batteries. That steep drop has made them the cheapest new power in many regions. Onshore wind or solar with a few hours of storage already has a lower levelized cost than gas peaking plants. Investors noticed. In 2021, renewables made up more than 80% of new electricity generating capacity.

nature-clim-216.title: Renewable energy sources
nature-clim-216.text: Hydropower is the largest renewable source of electricity, supplying 17% of the world's power in 2020. Renewable energy sources are those naturally replenished: solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, bioenergy and marine energy. They generally strengthen energy security and emit far fewer greenhouse gases than fossil fuels. Wind is catching up fast. It provided well over 10% of global electricity in 2024, and onshore wind is often cheaper than existing coal plants. Solar PV is expected to have the largest installed capacity of any electricity source by 2027. Renewables are not harmless, though. Projects can threaten biodiversity when high-value areas become bioenergy, wind or solar farms.

nature-clim-190.title: Coal phase-out
nature-clim-190.text: Coal is the most carbon-intensive fossil fuel. The IEA estimates it caused over 30% of warming above pre-industrial levels. Coal power emits about a tonne of CO2 per megawatt hour, twice as much as gas. Stopping coal burning in power plants and elsewhere is therefore central to the fossil fuel phase-out. Its health and environmental benefits exceed its costs, by over 1% of GDP a year according to one estimate. The IEA's 1.5°C pathway would require closing around 70% of existing coal capacity early. Germany uses reverse auctions to pay coal plants to close early, and some countries retire coal miners early. Economists have suggested a Coasean bargain, in which developed countries help pay for developing countries' phase-out. The 2021 Glasgow Climate Pact agreed to a coal phase-down.

nature-clim-176.title: Climate policy and stranded fossil assets
nature-clim-176.text: A 2021 study found that nearly 60 percent of oil and gas reserves and 90 percent of coal reserves must stay unused for a 50 percent chance of 1.5°C. Those reserves would lose their value. Climate-related asset stranding is this loss of value for fossil fuel reserves and carbon-intensive plants as policy, technology and markets shift. It hits oil, gas and coal companies, industries such as steel, aluminium and cement, and fossil-exporting countries and workers. Risk factors include environmental change, carbon pricing, falling clean-tech costs, changing social norms and litigation. A 2026 estimate found early closure of coal plants for a 1.5°C pathway would strand around $842 billion. Fossil fuel importers gain from switching, while exporters face the losses.

nature-clim-173.title: 100% renewable energy
nature-clim-173.text: Could every bit of energy come from renewable resources? That is the goal of 100% renewable energy. It is motivated by emissions, pollution, and economic and energy security concerns. The research is fairly young, with few studies before 2009.

nature-clim-170.title: Critical minerals for the energy transition
nature-clim-170.text: The IEA lists 37 critical minerals for clean energy technologies, and expects demand for them to rise 235 per cent by 2050. For mineral-rich countries of Sub-Saharan Africa, that boom may drive sustainable development. It has a cost. Mining for these minerals can threaten conservation areas, and in 2023 it contributed strongly to deforestation.

nature-clim-168.title: Transition or addition?
nature-clim-168.text: Has humanity ever really switched energy sources? One school, described by Vaclav Smil, sees successive transitions in the shares of the energy mix: biomass, then coal, then oil, then a mix. Jean-Baptiste Fressoz's school disagrees. It notes that 19th-century coal did not replace wood, because more wood was burned too. On this view, new sources are simply added on top of old ones. As of 2024, use of every form of primary energy had increased, leading some to call 'transition' a slogan. Historians still disagree.

nature-clim-171.title: The geopolitics of the energy transition
nature-clim-171.text: Changing energy sources changes the fortunes of countries and companies. Owners of fossil or renewable resources face big losses or gains, depending on how the transition unfolds. The shift is expected to reduce reliance on long-distance fossil fuel trade and raise the role of regional markets. Security matters too: energy security became a stronger driver in Europe after the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine.

nature-clim-219.title: Clean cooking
nature-clim-219.text: Cooking with biomass, together with fossil fuel pollution, causes an estimated 7 million deaths a year. Clean cooking replaces polluting fuels such as wood and dung with clean facilities. Polluting fuels release harmful smoke and can drive forest degradation. Universal clean cooking would greatly improve health with minimal effect on climate.

nature-clim-220.title: Paying for the energy transition
nature-clim-220.text: The energy transition needs investment of about 2.5% of world GDP, small compared with its economic and health benefits, most studies find. Raising that money is uneven. Underfunding is acute in least developed countries, which attract little private investment. Developed countries' Paris pledge of an extra $100 billion a year for poor countries has not been met. Money could also be freed. Ending fossil fuel subsidies could cut global carbon emissions by 28% and air pollution deaths by 46%.

nature-clim-218.title: Hydrogen: a fuel for the hardest jobs
nature-clim-218.text: Almost all hydrogen today comes from fossil fuels by steam methane reforming, emitting 6.6–9.3 tonnes of CO2 per tonne of hydrogen. Cleanly made hydrogen could instead serve as a fuel where cheaper low-carbon options are scarce, such as heavy industry and long-distance transport. Splitting water with clean electricity gives sustainable hydrogen, but it costs more and wastes much energy in conversion. It can supply the intense heat for steel, cement and glass, and replace coke in steelmaking.

nature-clim-217.title: Is bioenergy really green?
nature-clim-217.text: Biomass can be burned for heat and power or made into biofuels such as biodiesel and ethanol. Whether this cuts emissions depends on how the biomass is grown and sourced. Land-use change, cultivation and processing can make bioenergy emit more carbon overall than fossil fuels. Energy crops can displace ecosystems, degrade soils, use water and compete with food. Algae, waste and crops on land unfit for food are relatively sustainable sources. Its climate benefit is therefore contested, case by case.

nature-clim-188.title: What counts as 'unabated' fossil fuel?
nature-clim-188.text: Should the world phase out all fossil fuels, or only 'unabated' ones, burned without measures such as carbon capture that substantially cut emissions? Negotiators have argued over exactly this. The 2023 UN climate conference agreed to phase down unabated coal but left 'abated' undefined, which critics say invites abuse. The IPCC counts power plants as abated only if they capture 90% or more of emissions. Countries still disagree on the scope of phase-out targets.

nature-clim-195.title: Electrifying heat
nature-clim-195.text: Heat pumps provide only 5% of global space and water heating, the IEA estimates, but could provide over 90%. Heating electrification switches space, water and industrial heating from burning fuels to electricity, mainly heat pumps. Some industrial processes need very high temperatures, such as 900 °C for ethylene, and require new electric processes. The need is social too. Many households cannot afford enough heating or cooling, and existing heating is often polluting.

nature-clim-194.title: Electrifying transport
nature-clim-194.text: Producing electricity sustainably is easier than producing liquid fuels sustainably. That is the case for transport electrification: replacing fuel-burning vehicles with electric ones. Not every vehicle fits. Hydrogen may suit long-distance lorries, while shipping and aviation may rely more on sustainable liquid fuels.

nature-clim-198.title: Ending sales of petrol and diesel cars
nature-clim-198.text: Many countries have set dates to stop selling new petrol and diesel cars, requiring new cars to be electric or otherwise zero-emission. Many US states have zero-emission vehicle mandates requiring a rising share of electric car sales. Gas burning has no such deadline: no timetable exists for ending it.

nature-clim-191.title: Peak coal
nature-clim-191.text: Coal's share of global energy peaked in 2008 at 30%. Peak coal is the point of highest coal consumption, after which use is expected to decline. It was once expected to come from running out of reserves. Now falling demand drives it, as climate policy and cheaper gas and renewables spread. Use is falling in the US and Europe but rising in India, Indonesia and China.

reviews.mitigation-and-carbon-removal: Mitigation starts from a carbon budget: warming rises almost in a straight line with cumulative CO2, so only so much more can be emitted. Most of the work is cutting emissions, by phasing out fossil fuels, electrifying transport and heat, and building on wind, solar and batteries whose costs fell 55–85% in a decade. Net zero then needs carbon dioxide removal for what remains, from forests and biochar to direct air capture, though storage permanence, cost and the risk of delaying cuts are all disputed. Throughout, fairness decides who cuts and who pays, from splitting carbon budgets among nations to a just transition for workers and the energy poor.
